351.title: Count the stars (Genesis 15:1–6)
351.hook: childless and old, Abram is taken outside: count the stars
351.howItsDone: Genesis 15:6 is central to Christian teaching on faith: Paul quotes it in Romans 4 and Galatians 3, and James 2 quotes it too, and it is often preached on when churches talk about faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Melchizedek, a priest-king who met Abram with a meal and vanished. Your line: bread and wine and blessing.

Some promises get harder to believe the longer you wait. The job that was coming. The test results that would be fine. The baby that would come someday. Abram has been promised a great nation, children like the dust of the earth. Years have gone by. He's won a war, rescued Lot, been blessed by a king. But his tent is still quiet. No son, no daughter. And one night, God speaks to him again in a vision, and this time Abram talks back. Not with a song of praise. With the thing that's been keeping him up at night.
screen: `PROMISES HARDER TO BELIEVE.` → `HIS TENT IS STILL QUIET.` → `ABRAM TALKS BACK.`

segments.voice: God opens with comfort, in the King James Bible: "Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward." And Abram answers, honestly: what will you give me, seeing I go childless? My heir is a servant born in my house. It's not polite. It's real. And God doesn't scold him. Instead God does something simple. God brings him outside. An old man stepping out of his tent into a desert night, with no city lights anywhere, the whole sky crowded. "Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them: and he said unto him, So shall thy seed be." Tell the stars means count them. He can't, of course. Nobody could. Then comes the sentence the rest of the chapter turns on: "And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness." Believed. In Hebrew, he'emin, from the root aman, to be firm, to hold steady. It's the root of the very first word on this hill: amen. Abram said amen to the stars. He leaned his weight on a promise he still couldn't see. Remember Romans, a few weeks ago? Paul quotes this verse in chapter four: Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness. He quotes it again in Galatians, and the letter of James quotes it too. It starts with an old man outside his tent, trying to count.

segments.voice: If it's dark where you are, look up at the night sky, or picture the clearest one you've seen, and try to count: notice how fast you give up, and how more appear the longer you look. Then hold a promise you're still waiting on under those stars, without forcing it. If you pray, you can say amen to it.
Amen. The Hebrew root for believed, to be firm: what Abram said to a promise he couldn't see, so shall thy seed be.
Your line: so shall your seed be. He couldn't count them, and he believed. See you tomorrow.

352.title: The God who sees me (Genesis 16)
352.hook: Hagar, a runaway slave, is found by God at a spring and names him the God who sees
352.howItsDone: Many Christians pray to God as El Roi, the God who sees, especially in seasons of loneliness or mistreatment, and Hagar's story is often told in ministries that serve women, migrants and people in hardship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amen: an old man under a crowded sky, leaning on a promise. Your line: so shall your seed be.

Ten years in the land, and still no child. So Sarai makes a plan: she gives her Egyptian slave, Hagar, to Abram, so that a child born to Hagar would count as Sarai's. The story never gives Hagar a say in any of it. She becomes pregnant, and then everything goes wrong. Hagar looks down on Sarai. Sarai blames Abram. Abram says, she's your slave, do what you like. Sarai treats her harshly, and Hagar runs. A pregnant woman, alone, heading into the desert toward Egypt, toward home. Nobody in the household goes after her. But someone does.
screen: `TEN YEARS, STILL NO CHILD.` → `HAGAR HAS NO SAY.` → `SHE RUNS INTO THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: By a spring of water in the wilderness, on the road to Shur, the angel of the LORD finds her: an Egyptian slave girl on the run. And he does something nobody in the story has done. He calls her by name. In the King James Bible: "Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go?" Where have you come from, where are you going: the questions you ask a person, not property. She answers honestly: I'm running away. What he says next is hard. He tells her to go back and submit to Sarai. It's a hard line, and the text doesn't explain it. But he also gives her a promise like Abram's: descendants too many to count. And a name for her son: Ishmael, which means God hears, "because the LORD hath heard thy affliction." Then Hagar does something remarkable. She names God. "And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me." In Hebrew, El Roi, the God who sees me. An enslaved foreign woman with no power at all gives God a name. And the well there was called Beer-lahai-roi, the text says, because of what she said. Christians, and the Jews and Muslims who also remember Hagar, have found in this scene something steady. The person the household didn't see, the story says, God saw.

segments.voice: Think about someone around you who's easy not to see, the person who cleans the office after hours, the new kid, the relative everyone talks over, and picture their face: do you know their name, where they've come from, where they're going? If you pray, you can pray for them by name, or by the name you don't know yet. If you don't, just hold their face in mind for a while.
El Roi. The God who sees me. The name Hagar, a runaway slave, gives to God at a spring in the desert.
Your line: you are seen. The one nobody went after was found. Day three hundred fifty-two.

353.title: Three strangers at Mamre (Genesis 18:1–15)
353.hook: Abraham runs to feed three visitors, and Sarah laughs behind the tent
353.howItsDone: Hospitality to strangers is a long Christian practice, from monasteries that receive every guest as Christ to churches that run open tables, and Rublev's icon of the three visitors hangs in many Orthodox homes and churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, El Roi, the name Hagar gave God at a spring. Your line: you are seen.

The hottest part of the day, in the hill country near Hebron. Nobody travels at noon if they can help it. Abraham, with the new name God has given him, is sitting at the door of his tent by the great trees of Mamre. He's ninety-nine years old. He looks up, and there are three men standing near him. Strangers. No warning, no dust cloud on the road. Just there. What he does next turns a hot afternoon into a feast.
screen: `NOON, IN THE HEAT OF THE DAY.` → `NINETY-NINE, AT THE TENT DOOR.` → `THREE STRANGERS, JUST THERE.`

segments.voice: He runs. A ninety-nine-year-old man, in the heat, runs to meet them and bows to the ground. And then listen to how modest his offer is, in the King James Bible: "Let a little water, I pray you, be fetched, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree: And I will fetch a morsel of bread." A little water, a morsel of bread. And then he hurries. He tells Sarah to make cakes from a huge amount of fine flour. He runs to the herd for a tender calf. Butter, milk, meat. A morsel turns into a feast, and he stands by them under the tree while they eat. Then one of them asks: where is Sarah thy wife? And promises that by this time next year, Sarah will have a son. Sarah is listening behind the tent door. She's around ninety. And she laughs, quietly, to herself: worn out as I am, and my husband old, shall I have this pleasure now? The visitor hears it. Why did Sarah laugh? And then the question at the center of today: "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?" In Hebrew, too hard is too wonderful, from the word pele, a wonder, beyond reach. Sarah, afraid, says I didn't laugh. The answer: "Nay; but thou didst laugh." Who are these three? The text moves between three men and the LORD speaking. Some Christian readers have seen a hint of the Trinity here; Andrei Rublev's Orthodox icon paints the three seated around one table. Jewish tradition reads the three as angels, with God appearing to Abraham. And the New Testament letter to the Hebrews draws its own lesson: some have entertained angels unawares.

segments.voice: Think of the next person who'll come to your door, your desk or your table, and picture Abraham's way of meeting them: getting up, going to meet them, offering water before they ask, something to eat, a place to sit. Small, but more than they expect. If you pray, you can pray for whoever comes next.

Your line: is anything too hard? A morsel of bread can turn into a feast. Day three hundred fifty-three, done.

354.title: Abraham bargains (Genesis 18:16–33)
354.hook: fifty righteous? forty-five? ten? He argues with God for a city
354.howItsDone: Many Christians pray intercessions for cities and nations in trouble, and many churches include prayers for the world and for places in the news in their weekly worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pele, a wonder: a feast at noon and Sarah laughing behind the tent door. Your line: is anything too hard?

Haggle in a market, and you know the rhythm. You name a price. They name a price. You come down a little; they come up a little. Somebody pretends to walk away. Now try it with God. After the meal at Mamre, the visitors look out toward Sodom, down on the plain where Lot lives. And God, the story says, decides not to hide from Abraham what is about to happen: the outcry against Sodom is great, and God is going down to see. The two others walk on. Abraham stays, and steps closer.
screen: `NAME A PRICE, COME DOWN A LITTLE.` → `LOOKING DOWN TOWARD SODOM.` → `ABRAHAM STEPS CLOSER.`

segments.voice: His first words are a question: will you destroy the righteous with the wicked? Suppose there are fifty righteous people in the city. Then the line that sits at the center of the whole chapter, in the King James Bible: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?" Abraham is holding God to God's own justice. And God agrees: for fifty, I'll spare the whole place. Then the haggling begins. Abraham knows exactly how bold he's being. He says: "Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes." Dust: remember the garden. A creature of dust, arguing with his maker. What about forty-five? Yes. Forty? Yes. Thirty? Twenty? Each time God agrees, without a single complaint. Then the last one: oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak yet but this once. Ten? "I will not destroy it for ten's sake." And there Abraham stops. Notice two things. He isn't only bargaining for Lot; Lot's name never comes up. He's arguing for a whole city of strangers, wicked ones at that. And God never rebukes him for it. Abraham isn't the last to argue with God in the Bible. Moses will plead for his people. Job will demand an answer. Whole psalms ask how long, O LORD. The Bible keeps room for this kind of honest, bold prayer, right alongside thy will be done. The text says God stayed in the conversation until Abraham was done.

segments.voice: Think of a place that's hurting, a city in the news, a neighborhood near you, a hospital ward, and hold the whole place in mind, strangers included. If you pray, you can speak up for it as Abraham did, plainly, even stubbornly, and ask again. If you don't, hold it with the same stubborn care, and notice what you'd ask for if you could.
Abraham bargains. Fifty, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten: a man of dust and ashes argues with God for a whole city, and God listens.

355.title: Isaac means laughter (Genesis 21:1–7)
355.hook: God has made me laugh, says Sarah at ninety
355.howItsDone: Many Christians speak of Sarah and Abraham as models of faith in God's promises, following the letter to the Hebrews, which praises Sarah for judging God faithful to his promise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abraham bargained, from fifty down to ten, for a city of strangers. Your line: you can argue with god.

There's a kind of laugh you can't help. The one that bursts out when the impossible thing actually happens: the test comes back clear, the acceptance letter after years of no, the friend you thought you'd lost, standing at the door. In Genesis, laughter keeps turning up around one promise. Abraham laughed when God first said Sarah would have a son; he fell on his face and laughed, the text says, at ninety-nine. Sarah, listening at the tent door, laughed to herself. Both laughed because it was too much to believe. Today, they find out how it ends.
screen: `THE LAUGH YOU CAN'T HELP.` → `ABRAHAM LAUGHED. SARAH LAUGHED.` → `TOO MUCH TO BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: Chapter twenty-one opens almost quietly, in the King James Bible: "And the LORD visited Sarah as he had said." As he had said. Twenty-five years after the call to go, the promise lands. Sarah, around ninety, has a son, and Abraham, a hundred, names him Isaac, just as he'd been told. And the name is the joke, and the joy. In Hebrew, Isaac is Yitzchak, which means he laughs. Every time anyone says this boy's name for the rest of his life, they'll be saying laughter. Then Sarah speaks: "God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me." Think about how far she's come. At the tent door at Mamre, her laugh was a disbelieving one, quiet, to herself, and then denied out of fear. Now it's out loud, and it's for everyone. All that hear will laugh with me. She goes on: who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? I've borne him a son in his old age. The same word, laugh, carries both meanings in this story: the laugh of doubt, and the laugh of joy. The text doesn't erase the first one. It turns it around. Christians have often seen in Isaac's birth a picture of God doing what people think is impossible, and the letter to the Hebrews praises Sarah's faith in it. But the scene itself isn't a sermon. It's an old woman holding a baby, laughing, and inviting everyone to laugh with her.

segments.voice: Think of a moment when something you'd given up on actually happened, or the funniest thing that happened this month, and let yourself smile at it. If a laugh comes, let it out, even alone, and notice how it feels in your body. If you pray, you can give thanks for the joke and the joy.

356.title: Hagar in the wilderness (Genesis 21:8–21)
356.hook: cast out with her son, Hagar sits a bowshot away, and God opens her eyes to a well
356.howItsDone: Many Christians turn to Hagar's story in times of exile, abandonment or single parenthood, and some churches and ministries for women and refugees take her well as a sign that God sees and provides.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yitzchak, he laughs: Sarah holding a son at last. Your line: god made me laugh.

The laughter doesn't last long in Abraham's tent. At the feast for Isaac's weaning, Sarah sees Ishmael, Hagar's son, mocking, the King James says; other translations say laughing, or playing. She says to Abraham: cast out this bondwoman and her son. The text says the thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight, because of his son. But God tells him to listen to Sarah, and promises that Ishmael too will become a nation. So early in the morning, Abraham gives Hagar some bread and a skin of water, puts it on her shoulder, and sends them away. Into the desert, again.
screen: `A FEAST, AND A LAUGH THAT CUTS.` → `CAST OUT THIS BONDWOMAN.` → `BREAD, A SKIN OF WATER, THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: Hagar wanders in the wilderness of Beersheba until the water runs out. Then comes the hardest picture in her story. She puts the boy under a bush, and in the King James Bible: "she went, and sat her down over against him a good way off, as it were a bowshot: for she said, Let me not see the death of the child." A bowshot: close enough to be near him, far enough not to watch. And she lifts up her voice and weeps. But listen to what the next verse says: "And God heard the voice of the lad." Remember his name from the first time Hagar ran? Ishmael, God hears. The name comes true again. The angel of God calls to her out of heaven: what aileth thee, Hagar? fear not. Get up, lift the boy, hold him by the hand. And then: "And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water." The text doesn't say God made a well appear. It says God opened her eyes. Was it there all along, a bowshot away, and grief had kept her from seeing it? The text doesn't settle it, but some readers hear it that way. She fills the skin and gives the boy a drink. The story ends with this: "God was with the lad." He grows up in the wilderness, becomes an archer, and his mother finds him a wife from Egypt. The household had sent them away. God had not. Muslims remember Hagar and Ishmael too, and tell their own story of her search for water. In Genesis, it ends at a well she hadn't seen.

segments.voice: Think of a place where you feel the water's run out, money, energy, patience, hope, and notice where you've sat down a bowshot away. Then look slowly around it, as if your eyes could be opened: a person who's offered, a rest you haven't taken. If you pray, you can ask for your eyes to be opened.
Ishmael. Hebrew for God hears: the name that comes true when God hears the boy's cries in the wilderness and Hagar's eyes are opened.
Your line: there's a well. Sometimes it's closer than grief lets you see. See you tomorrow.

357.title: The mountain of Moriah (Genesis 22:1–19)
357.hook: the hardest story: Abraham is tested, a ram is caught, and the place is named the Lord will provide
357.howItsDone: Many churches read Genesis 22 during Lent or at the Easter Vigil, where it is heard alongside the story of Good Friday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ishmael, God hears, and a well Hagar couldn't see. Your line: there's a well.

Some stories you can tell a child at bedtime. Some you can't. Genesis twenty-two is the second kind. Jews call it the Akedah, the binding. Christians, Jews and Muslims each have their own tellings of a father asked to give up his son. Painters and philosophers keep coming back to it. It is a hard text, and rereading doesn't make it softer. So today isn't about solving it; it's about reading it slowly and sitting with it.
screen: `NOT A BEDTIME STORY.` → `THE AKEDAH, THE BINDING.` → `NOT SOLVING IT, SITTING WITH IT.`

segments.voice: It opens, in the King James Bible: "God did tempt Abraham." Tempt here means test, and the reader is told that before Abraham knows anything. God calls, and Abraham answers, here am I. Then the command, every phrase heavier than the last: "Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest." Go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there. Early in the morning, Abraham saddles his donkey, and they walk for three days. Isaac carries the wood. Abraham carries the fire and the knife. Isaac: "Behold the fire and the wood: but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" Abraham: "My son, God will provide himself a lamb." And the two of them went together, the text says, twice. At the top, Abraham builds the altar, binds his son, and lifts the knife, and the angel of the LORD calls his name twice: Abraham, Abraham. Lay not thine hand upon the lad. He looks up, and there is a ram caught in a thicket by its horns. He names the place Jehovah-jireh, in the King James Bible: the LORD will see, the LORD will provide. In Hebrew it's the same verb as Hagar's El Roi, the God who sees. Readers answer it in many ways. Jews read it at the new year and remember Abraham's faith and Isaac's binding. Christian tradition has heard Good Friday in it: a son carrying wood up a hill, and a lamb provided. And readers in each tradition have found it deeply troubling. The text doesn't say what Abraham felt, how old Isaac was, or whether Sarah knew. That's the end of a week of promises: stars, a seeing God, strangers, a bargain, a laugh, a well, and this mountain.
screen: `GOD DID TEMPT: GOD TESTED.` · `WHERE IS THE LAMB?` · `A RAM CAUGHT IN A THICKET.` · `YIREH: THE LORD WILL SEE.` · then, large: `GOD WILL PROVIDE HIMSELF A LAMB.`

segments.voice: You don't have to make sense of Moriah today; let it sit, unresolved, like a stone in your hand, beside anything in your own life you can't tie up. Don't argue it closed or force a moral; keep breathing next to it, the way father and son walked together. If you pray, you can bring it to God as it is.
Jehovah-jireh. The name Abraham gives the mountain: the Lord will see, the Lord will provide, after a ram is caught and Isaac is spared.
Your line: the lord will provide. A hard question can stay a question for now. That's the week.
